title: Rhetorical Synthesis, Part 2: A Hard Question and Traps

beats.say: In part one, we learned to read the goal first, and to turn it into a short checklist.
beats.item: Read the goal; make a checklist

beats.say: Then we checked each choice against the checklist. All four choices were true, so we eliminated by the goal.
In this video, we work through a hard question about an audience, and then the common traps.
beats.item: Today: a hard question and traps

beats.say: Hard question. When the goal says the audience is unfamiliar with a topic, the sentence must say what the topic is. A term used without explanation fails.

card.sub: Name it and say what it is

beats.say: A goal can also have two parts, such as a difference and a similarity. Then the sentence needs both parts.

scenes.title: The student's notes
scenes.text: A kilim is a flat-woven rug. Kilims are made by weaving colored threads across a frame, without tying knots. Many kilims come from Turkey, and their bold geometric patterns often carry symbolic meanings. Knotted rugs are thicker, because each knot adds a tuft of yarn.

beats.say: Suppose the goal is to introduce kilims to an audience that has never heard of them. The checklist is, the name, and what it is.
beats.underline: A kilim is a flat-woven rug

beats.say: The best sentence should name the kilim, and say it is a flat-woven rug made without knots. A detail like Turkey is optional.

scenes.title: Which sentence meets the goal?
scenes.question: Which choice most effectively introduces kilims to an audience unfamiliar with them?

options.A: Many kilims come from Turkey, where their bold patterns carry symbolic meanings.
options.B: Unlike knotted rugs, kilims are thin because no knots add tufts of yarn.
options.C: A kilim is a flat-woven rug made by weaving colored threads across a frame, without tying knots.
options.D: The patterns of a kilim are geometric and bold.

beats.say: Choice A talks about where kilims come from, and the meaning of their patterns. It never says what a kilim is, so a new reader would be lost.
Choice B compares kilims with knotted rugs. A new reader does not know either one, so the comparison does not introduce a kilim.
Choice D describes the patterns, but it never says that a kilim is a rug. An unfamiliar reader cannot tell what it is.
Choice C names the kilim, and says what it is and how it is made. The answer is C.
Now the traps. Each one is a way that a careful reader can still pick a wrong answer. We will see the trap, and then the habit that avoids it.
Trap one. The longest sentence, with the most facts, looks like the best one. But more facts is not better.
beats.wrong: the sentence with the most facts

beats.say: The right facts are better than more facts. Choose the sentence that meets the goal, even if it is short.
beats.right: the sentence that meets the goal

beats.say: Trap two. This is the main trap. Every wrong choice is accurate to the notes, so accuracy cannot be the test.
beats.wrong: it is true, so it must be right

beats.say: Test each choice against the goal that the question states, and not against the notes.
beats.right: does it do what the goal asks?

beats.say: Trap three. A compare or contrast goal needs both items. A sentence about only one of them cannot be the answer.
Look for a sentence that names both items, and shows how they relate.
beats.right: While saffron is X, turmeric is Y.

beats.say: Trap four. If the goal asks for a difference and a similarity, a sentence with only one of them is incomplete.
Write each part of the goal in your checklist, and tick them off one by one.
beats.right: they differ in source, yet share color

beats.say: Trap five. If the reader has never heard of the topic, a sentence that uses a term without explaining it fails.
beats.wrong_why: Does not say what a kilim is

beats.say: For a new reader, name the topic and say what it is, before you add details.
beats.right: A kilim is a flat-woven rug.

beats.say: To recap. All choices are true, so the goal decides. Use a checklist, and tick every part of the goal.
beats.item: The goal decides; use a checklist

beats.say: Mention both items in a comparison, and define the topic for an unfamiliar reader. In the next topic, we study boundaries.
